\section[\ar{رأس}]{\ar{رأس} (raʾs) — the head}

\label{lesson:AR-C11-ras}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} One more ancient Semitic root — and a word still hard at work in modern political vocabulary, the same way Latin's \emph{caput} is in English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The word}
\textbf{\ar{رأس}} (\emph{raʾs}) = "\textbf{head}" — an ancient Semitic root, cousin of Hebrew \textbf{\he{ראש}} (\emph{rosh}), the very word inside \textbf{Rosh Hashanah}, "head of the year."

\begin{culture}
Arabic builds \textbf{\ar{رئيس}} (\emph{raʾīs}), "\textbf{president, chief, head {[}of an organization{]}}," directly on this same root — literally "the one who is the head." That's exactly the move English makes with Latin \emph{caput}: \textbf{captain} ("head" of a unit), \textbf{capital} ("head" city). Different language families, the same very human idea — the person or place "at the head" is the one in charge.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "raʾs" — head{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "raʾīs" — president, literally "the head {[}one{]}"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the Hebrew cousin — "raʾs / rosh"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{\ar{رأس}} mean, and what's its Hebrew cousin? (\textbf{"Head"} — cousin of \textbf{rosh}, as in Rosh Hashanah.) What word is built on it for "president," and what does it literally mean? (\textbf{\ar{رئيس}} \emph{raʾīs}, "the head {[}one{]}" — the same "head = leader" idea as English \emph{captain/capital} from Latin \emph{caput}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\ar{يد}]{\ar{يد} (yad) — the hand}

\label{lesson:AR-C11-yad}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Some words wear their age lightly — worn down, reshaped, disguised. This one hasn't changed much at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The word}
\textbf{\ar{يد}} (\emph{yad}) = "\textbf{hand}" — a short, ancient Semitic root. Its Hebrew cousin is spelled and pronounced almost \textbf{identically}: \textbf{\he{יד}} (\emph{yad}). Where \emph{raʾs/rosh} show a family resemblance, \emph{yad/yad} is closer to twins — one of the more strikingly unchanged shared words across the whole Semitic family.

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "yad" — hand{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the Hebrew twin — "yad" — almost the same word{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: contrast — "raʾs/rosh" changed more than "yad/yad" did{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{\ar{يد}} mean? (\textbf{"Hand."}) How does it compare to its Hebrew cousin? (\textbf{Nearly identical} — both \emph{yad} — one of the more strikingly unchanged shared words across the Semitic family.)
\end{tcolorbox}
